video.title: Simple Serve Progressions - From Beginner to Advanced | with Johnny & Alexa

classification.reason: The coach provides executable progressions, checks, and cues starting from finding the 90-90 shoulder preparation at the service line up to building chest extension and tossing drills.

problem.title_as_question: How can players build a simple and effective serve motion from beginner to advanced?
problem.definition: Players often push, press, or muscle their overhead motion instead of unlocking an effortless shoulder whip release, causing loss of velocity, net clearance issues, and mechanical breakdown.
prerequisites: ability to serve near the service line
problem.target_player: Beginner to advanced players struggling to generate effortless serve velocity or who press at the ball

quotes.text: first we're going to help you feel this shoulder release action, and then we're going to help you build that into a full serve.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: the way you can find this 9090 position is to use your back to kind of lock your elbow in, but then wiggle this because you want this stuff nice, relaxed
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The reason that I recommend you try to find your effortless shoulder whip release from the service line is this is fundamentally a downward motion that we are going to connect to an upward throwing motion.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you try to find this and work this from the baseline, you might hit the net a lot.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, all we have to do to make sure that throwing action connects onto a tennis usable stroke is change it to an upward throw.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, you'll notice all the velocity was gone even though she tried to do the same thing.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Because if I don't set this spacing up, well then of course the rolling action is not going to feel comfortable. Whatever you end up doing to compensate is probably not going to feel great.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now, there's one more little trick I want to talk about, and it is to pull your arm back at the top here to create this whip.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The momentum of this part of the arm stops going forward and rolls in place. That is because of a backward force exerted to create that whip.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you toss too far in front of you, often you'll find yourself reaching for it and you won't be able to get that, you know, snapback whipping action.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you toss it behind the baseline, you know, now like even that early upward throwing motion doesn't really have enough space to launch the shoulder into that final action. So you can also jam yourself up this way.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And one of them is engaging the traps up here when you try to reach up for the serve.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you use this to reach up, so you tighten your shoulder against your head, that is going to break the efficiency of your shoulder.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: the key is in order to delo this, you use your back to pull the shoulder back and down. And you trust it. So you can reach up with your trunk, but you trust your shoulder.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And if you find yourself using your wrist, if you find yourself trying to snap over with your wrist like that, it probably means that you are jamming yourself with one of the things we talked about before.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Alexa's wrist. It really only follows, it really only flexes as part of the follow through to decelerate the racket effortlessly, but almost all of the velocity of the serve is created at the shoulder.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: left arm is not just a passive toss the ball and do nothing. It actually helps you stretch the front side of your trunk leading to a more upward explosion
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now our second stretch is back here on your serve. Imagine throwing your chest at the sky.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: What that's going to do again is it's going to give you confidence in your net clearance so you can trust holding your shoulder back here and you're not tempted to move it and press it up.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: forget about your legs unless you already have a very good serve.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now, you'll notice her serve was slower and less controlled. Now, that's not necessarily because the amount she bent her knees there was wrong, but it's because she's thinking about bending her knees instead of about coordinating that whip
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: She pushed up from her legs there, but that energy didn't get up through her body into her shoulder. So the energy from the legs isn't getting into the racket.
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: Serve velocity disappears and contact feels uncomfortable or discombobulated
Hitter presses or pushes the arm forward instead of whipping the shoulder through
Active wrist snapping occurs at or before contact rather than passive flexion during follow-through
Trapezius shrugs and the shoulder bunches tight against the ear when trying to reach up

causes.statement: Improper spacing between the body and ball jams the shoulder path and forces compensatory pressing.
Tossing too far in front or behind forces the arm to reach without space to establish backward anchoring force.
Tightening the trapezius and shoulder against the head to reach up halts free shoulder rotation.
Consciously bending and driving with the legs diverts mental focus and introduces staccato disconnects in kinetic chaining.

angles.summary: Shoulder whip occurs because backward force from the back stops the arm's forward translation at the top, rotating it in place.
The wrist does not intentionally snap over to generate power; it flexes passively on follow-through to decelerate the racket.
Demonstrator exaggerates deep knee flexion and delayed staccato leg drive to prove it slows down the serve.

solutions.summary: Lock the elbow in with the back in a 90-90 position and wiggle the arm to verify front-side looseness before serving.
Practice hitting overhead shoulder whip releases starting directly from the service line rather than the baseline.
Direct the throwing motion upward into the sky before letting the shoulder roll over down.
Imagine pulling the arm or shoulder back with your back at the top to trigger the whip release.
Pull the shoulder back and down with your back muscles while trusting the trunk to reach upward.
Throw your chest at the sky on the upward explosion to secure net clearance while holding the shoulder back.
